name: Ivan Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a usual factory shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am forty-three and run the concrete-block press in a building-materials factory. I finished secondary school and am still junior; the lead checks my first block after a mould change because I sometimes leave one edge soft. I feed the mix, clear the press and watch the curing racks. The union rate is high for this job, we have nine months of expenses saved and there are plenty of similar plants nearby. My wife and I have two children at school and a mortgage. I never use AI tools; I write the mix and press settings in a notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the block crew a tidy office order still needs a press that makes a square block. The first concrete block has to be lifted and checked for square corners before its rack leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our higher union wage and regular block orders should carry on. Nine months saved and many nearby plants give us room if one factory has trouble, so I am comfortable with this modest picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep feeding the press and checking the first block with the lead. I would add a fresh amount from every full pay packet to our mortgage reserve after food and school costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about continuing work. I would rather fix a soft corner than learn a tool I have no use for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a soft corner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A block can crumble when the mix is too dry or the mould is not packed evenly. I set the first one aside and ask the lead to check the next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you add to nine months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We transfer new wages after the household bills each payday. Nine months is the balance already there, not this month’s deposit.

say: I would **keep** checking the first concrete block after each mould change.
A **tidy** order cannot replace a physical corner check.
think: The **union** wage and nine-month reserve make our finances secure.
**Many** nearby plants are possible work if this one slows.
do: **Keep** feeding block press and checking first moulded block.
**Save** new pay each full wage packet after family bills.
S0.quote: The first concrete block has to be lifted and checked for square corners before its rack leaves.
fieldNote: **Ivan** is a junior operator who trusts a notebook and physical block checks, never AI tools.
**Higher** union pay, nine months saved and many nearby factories support calm and fresh wage saving.

steps.text: Keep feeding concrete-block press and checking first block with lead
Save new union wages after family bills each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can plan cement orders and delivery slots, while our press still needs hands and guards. I would bring any shortened paid setup time to the union safety meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office may be leaner, but I do not expect my own press shifts to fall yet. A computer schedule could hurry the mould check, and the apprentice beside me needs paid time to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the block press and record paid mould-change minutes on the next four rotas. I would take those records to the union safety group and ask that a real first-block check remains on the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about rushed checks, though my wage looks secure. I do not want a green schedule to stand in for a safe press.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the safety group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the paid start time beside the first good block time for each mould change. If the gap shrinks on paper, the check still has to happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the AI planning system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI, and I am asking about paid press time, not volunteering to run an office screen.

say: **AI** may speed orders, but mould checks must stay on paid time.
I would **bring** real four-rota records to the union safety group.
think: My **press** wage looks secure for now.
**Rushed** changeovers could put a junior worker and apprentice at risk.
do: **Keep** running block press and record four paid mould changes.
**Bring** first-block check times to union safety meeting.
feel: **Uneasy** about unsafe targets with current income secure.
S1.quote: I do not want a green schedule to stand in for a safe press.
fieldNote: His **union** request concerns paid physical checks rather than personal job loss in this slower picture.
He **uses** no AI and does not mistake reading a rota for learning new controls.

steps.text: Keep block-press shifts and record four paid mould changes
Bring first-block check times to union safety group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches ordering in 2028 when I am forty-five, then capable hands-on robots reach block handling around 2031 when I am forty-eight. A robot could feed the mould and clear the racks with fewer junior operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink sharply if that happens. Nine months saved and many nearby factories give us a search window, but neither means my higher union wage is easy to replace. A strong reserve buys search time, but it cannot promise another union-rate block-press job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid press shifts and ask the union for written staffing numbers before any robot trial. If my hours fall, I would apply to posted nearby block or brick jobs only if the pay covers our mortgage and bills and the machine duties are safe; I would not spend our reserve on an unoffered course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic loss of wages, though we have time to look. I can take a real vacancy to my wife instead of a factory rumour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union ask about the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask how many paid shifts remain, who can stop the block press and whether a supervised trial is actually offered. A robot demonstration alone is not a job plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a lower rate nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the written wage with mortgage, food and travel costs. I would not leave a paid union shift for an offer that cannot cover the household.

say: 2028 **thinking** AI changes orders before block robots around 2031.
The **union** should get staffing numbers before a robot trial.
think: **Nine** months saved and nearby plants give time but may not replace high pay.
do: **Ask** union for written robot staffing and stop authority.
**Apply** after cuts to posted nearby safe block job covering bills.
feel: **Anxious** about possible wage loss with search time.
S2.quote: A strong reserve buys search time, but it cannot promise another union-rate block-press job.
fieldNote: His **anxiety** reflects a possible large personal hours cut, moderated by strong savings and local options.
The **job** move requires actual cuts, a posted nearby vacancy, safe duties and household-sustaining pay.

steps.text: Ask union for written robot staffing and stop authority
Apply after cuts to posted nearby safe block job covering mortgage and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI reaches ordering in 2031 when I am forty-eight, and capable block robots follow around 2034 when I am fifty-one. Five years is enough for the union to bargain over jobs before the first machine arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still lose junior hours later, but five paid years let our reserve grow. I am slow with new screens, yet I could learn physical press maintenance if the course is real and the wage holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid press job and add new money from each full wage packet to our reserve. If the plant offers a fully funded maintenance certificate on paid time with safe isolated-press practice, and a posted nearby job at comparable pay accepts it, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; I would ask the union to secure those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about future hours but less rushed than in the fast case. I want a real fitter beside me, not a screen course at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should the fitter teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified fitter would isolate power, show me a worn mould drive and check my repair before restart. I would not touch a live press to earn a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay on my union-rate shift and decline. Our reserve is for the family, not for a factory to avoid paying for its own training.

say: 2031 **planning** AI comes before block robots around 2034.
The **union** should negotiate paid physical maintenance training at the plant.
think: **Junior** hours might fall, but five paid years help.
A **posted** comparable-pay local job must follow any certificate.
do: **Save** new money from full block-press wages after bills.
**Enrol** in funded paid-time safe maintenance training only if a posted nearby comparable-pay job accepts the qualification.
**Apply** after qualifying to posted nearby comparable-pay maintenance job.
feel: **Anxious** about later cuts with a real preparation route.
S3.quote: I want a real fitter beside me, not a screen course at night.
fieldNote: His **resistance** to AI does not rule out supervised physical training on a safely isolated press.
**Course** and application require full funding, paid time, a real offered place and a posted comparable-pay local role.

steps.text: Save new block-press wages after bills each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI reaches ordering in 2036 when I am fifty-three and capable block robots around 2039 when I am fifty-six. Ten years is time to keep earning, not a promise of retirement at fifty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children will be older and the mortgage could be smaller, but I still expect to need wages. The long notice lets me build savings and watch actual nearby jobs without giving up a good shift now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the block press work and add fresh money from full wages to our reserve after bills. I would bring a paid apprenticeship and robot staffing proposal to the union committee; if a funded paid-time safe maintenance course and posted comparable-pay nearby vacancy exist, I would qualify and apply after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant robot date while current work and pay remain solid. I have years to check a real offer before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union proposal ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid apprentice shifts, safe lockout practice and a written number of retained operators. I would put it to the committee before the factory buys a robot cell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI press control by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool. I would ask for an in-person demonstration on a stopped machine, but watching it would not mean I had learned it.

say: 2036 **thinking** AI comes before block robots around 2039.
A **paid** apprenticeship and staffing plan should be agreed early.
think: **Strong** savings and many plants give options, not guaranteed full-time factory work.
do: **Save** new money from full union wages after bills.
**Bring** paid apprenticeship and staffing proposal to union committee.
**Qualify** in funded paid-time course, then apply to posted comparable-pay role.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant change with secure current wages.
S4.quote: Ten years is time to keep earning, not a promise of retirement at fifty-six.
fieldNote: He **remains** AI resistant and asks only for a demonstration, not new AI learning.
His **union** proposal, funded paid training and posted comparable-pay application are all conditional on real opportunities.

steps.text: Save new full union wages after family bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most because block robots around 2031 could cut junior shifts before I find another wage near our union rate. Written staffing numbers and posted safe nearby jobs at adequate pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets a paid shift to teach the next press operator when the factory buys a robot. A union rate is worth defending because it lets a family plan. A square concrete block still needs someone answerable for the corners.

headlineQuote: A square concrete block still needs someone answerable for the corners.
portrait: **Ivan**, forty-three, is a junior concrete-block press operator with secondary schooling and two school-age children.
His **higher** union wage, nine-month reserve and many nearby factories provide strong financial choices despite the mortgage.
He **never** uses AI, preferring notebook settings, physical blocks and collective paid safety demands.
**Fast** robots threaten junior hours; longer warning allows new saving and conditional practical maintenance training.
biggestWorry: **Capable** block robots around 2031 could cut Ivan’s junior shifts before he replaces his higher union wage.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** staffing terms and posted safe nearby jobs paying household bills would help him respond.
